object.text: Consider that Earth has been sculpting itself for exactly 4.5 billion years—a span so vast that the entire arc of human civilization, from the first crude settlements along the Euphrates to the digital networks encircling the globe, occupies less than the final ten-thousandth of one percent of that history. Long before any person observed them, supercontinents merged and fractured, seas expanded and contracted, and peaks ascended only to be eroded into silt. Countless organisms rose to prominence and eventually disappeared, leaving behind nothing but subtle chemical traces embedded in geological strata. Even the iron circulating in our veins originated within dying stars prior to the planet's formation from cosmic debris. In this context, our most lasting structures, ancient scripts, and established systems are merely transient sparks during an eternal tempest. This immense scale of time is not an act of malice, but a reminder of how unlikely our existence is and that the world's narrative is not centered on humanity. We have arrived late, resting upon a historical abyss that we can categorize but never fully comprehend.

Consider that Earth has been sculpting itself for exactly 4.5 billion years—a span so vast that the entire arc of human civilization, from the first crude settlements along the Euphrates to the digital networks encircling the globe, occupies less than the final ten-thousandth of one percent of that history. Mountains have risen and been ground to sand, oceans have opened and closed like slow-breathing lungs, entire supercontinents have assembled and torn apart, all without a single human witness. Species beyond counting have flourished, dominated, and vanished into stone, their existence remembered only by the faintest chemical whispers pressed between layers of rock. The very iron in our blood was forged inside collapsing stars long before this planet coalesced from interstellar dust. Against this backdrop, our proudest monuments, our oldest written languages, our most enduring institutions are scarcely a flicker—a momentary electrical discharge in a storm that has been raging for eons. Deep time does not diminish us out of cruelty; it simply reveals the staggering improbability of our presence and the humbling truth that the Earth does not revolve around our story. We are latecomers, perched on a depth of history we can name but never truly fathom.
